name: Burru and Nyabinghi
text: Burru drumming, a Jamaican tradition with deep African roots, was played in the poorest parts of Kingston. Rastas in the West Kingston yards took it up and joined it to their chants and hymns. The result became the Nyabinghi style: three drums, a heartbeat pulse, and worship that could last all night.
listen: Ras Michael & the Sons of Negus: Nyabinghi chants

name: Count Ossie and Wareika Hill
text: Oswald Williams, known as Count Ossie, ran a Rasta camp in the Wareika Hills above east Kingston. Jazz players and drummers came up the hill to play and reason together. In 1960 the producer Prince Buster brought Ossie's drummers into the studio for the Folkes Brothers' “Oh Carolina”: Rasta drums on a Jamaican pop record for the first time.
listen: The Folkes Brothers with Count Ossie: Oh Carolina
Count Ossie & the Mystic Revelation of Rastafari: Grounation (1973)

name: Ska
text: As Jamaica moved to independence in 1962, ska became its sound. Many of its finest players, including members of the Skatalites, had spent time in Rasta camps, and Ethiopian and African themes ran through the instrumental titles of the era. The movement's influence was in the musicians before it was in the lyrics.
listen: Don Drummond: trombone features with the Skatalites

name: Roots reggae
text: In the 1970s Rasta theology moved to the front of the music. Burning Spear sang Garvey's prophecies, the Abyssinians wrote a hymn that is still sung at gatherings, and Culture's “Two Sevens Clash”, tied to a prophecy attributed to Garvey, made so many people nervous that much of Kingston shut down on 7 July 1977.
listen: Bob Marley & the Wailers: Rastaman Chant

name: Dub
text: Engineers such as King Tubby and Lee “Scratch” Perry stripped songs back to drum and bass, then filled the space with echo and reverb. Many listeners hear dub as meditation: the voice falls away and the heartbeat remains, close to the feel of a Nyabinghi Issembly.
listen: King Tubby: dub versions from the mid-1970s
Augustus Pablo: King Tubbys Meets Rockers Uptown

name: Britain's sound systems
text: In Britain, Rastafari spread through sound systems as much as through records. Jah Shaka's system in south London played spiritual, heavy music for decades and treated a dance as a kind of service. Steel Pulse from Handsworth and Aswad from west London gave young Black Britons a Rasta voice of their own.
listen: Jah Shaka: Commandments of Dub series

name: Dancehall turns to fire
text: In the 1990s, a wave of dancehall artists turned to Rastafari. Buju Banton's “'Til Shiloh” (1995) marked his change; Sizzla, Capleton and Anthony B brought Bobo Shanti turbans and “fire” imagery to a global audience. Some lyrics from this era drew international criticism and boycotts over homophobic content, a debate that still divides listeners, including Rastas.
listen: Capleton and Anthony B: late-1990s singles

name: The Reggae Revival
text: A new generation brought roots music back to Jamaica's centre. Chronixx, Protoje, Jesse Royal, Kabaka Pyramid and Jah9, one of the most prominent Rasta women in music, made conscious reggae popular again. In 2018 UNESCO added the reggae music of Jamaica to its list of the intangible cultural heritage of humanity, noting its role in giving voice to the marginalised and in praising God.
